classification_vocabulary.PIT_VERIFIED: primary-source evidence fixes both the value identity and an availability time on or before the decision instant, with no measured restatement affecting a decision
classification_vocabulary.PIT_CONSERVATIVE_PROXY: availability is a declared convention or the series shows measured backfill, so the value used is conservative rather than provable
classification_vocabulary.PIT_FAILED: a decision demonstrably consumed a value published after its instant

defillama_stablecoin.declared_convention: value dated day t treated as available 00:00 UTC of day t+1
defillama_stablecoin.why: the payload carries no publication timestamp, so decision-time availability is a declared convention rather than a vendor fact; the convention is one full day of conservatism and no settled history moved in the observed re-fetch window

decision_time_rules.stablecoin_cutoff: most recent daily value dated at or before Sunday-2 (one day of availability lag)
decision_time_rules.macro_cutoff: most recent complete Wednesday snapshot, whose H.4.1 inputs publish the following Thursday
decision_time_rules.execution: first daily bar open strictly after the decision instant (Monday 00:00 UTC)

not_yet_decidable_decisions.rule: a decision with no usable value is FLAT; that is fail-closed behaviour, not look-ahead

incremental_reconstruction.method: the decision is recomputed from a feed truncated at the decision instant and compared with the full-history value; equality means the signal is a function of past data only

def_htf_pit_001_assessment.reason: both frozen rules consume completed daily values and closed weekly references; no higher-timeframe bar is read while still forming, and execution is deferred to the next bar open

composite_classification.note: the weaker of a hypothesis's inputs decides its composite class

residual_risks: the stablecoin series has no vendor publication timestamp: the t+1 convention is the mitigation, and the sealed-period collector must read the settled value and retain the retrieval record

mechanisms.shared_label: both sit in a 'dollar liquidity -> risk appetite' family; the information sets and the transmission channels differ, and the frozen cross-incremental test is the control

hypothesis_independence.conclusion: the two candidates do not trade the same clock: different inputs, different sampling frequency and different transmission channels. The measured state overlap is reported above; it is a structural measure, not an economic one, and the frozen cross-incremental test remains the decisive control (if either candidate is indistinguishable from the other's state, the frozen test rejects it).

sample_feasibility.method: frozen rules applied to research-exposed inputs; only trade counts and dates are produced. No return, no PnL and no profit factor is computed, and the sealed window is untouched.
sample_feasibility.statistical_criterion_unchanged: 20 round trips or 24 months, whichever comes first; fewer than 20 at 24 months is INSUFFICIENT_OOS_SAMPLE and is neither PASS nor REJECT

H-049-001.frozen_floor: 20 closed round trips or 24 months, whichever comes first

H-049-002.declared_development_start: first decidable week (on or after 2004-01-01) to 2023-12-31 (RESEARCH_EXPOSED for price; the FRED series were never used by any prior campaign)
H-049-002.frozen_floor: 20 closed round trips or 24 months, whichever comes first

sample_feasibility.conclusion: the frozen count floor is reachable inside the sealed window only if the realised turnover matches the measured exposed-history turnover. Where it does not, the correct outcome is INSUFFICIENT_OOS_SAMPLE, and the sample floor must not be lowered to manufacture a verdict.

verified_record.title: The Relationship Between Stablecoin and Cryptocurrency Returns During Periods of Market Stress
verified_record.abstract: Active asset managers increasingly include cryptocurrencies in their alternative asset allocations, highlighting their speculative and volatile nature. The aim of this research is to examine trends in the returns and volatility of cryptocurrencies, whilst accounting for the depegging of stablecoins, driven by speculative trading during macroeconomic shocks and technological shifts. We build a sample of market capitalisation, using data from the daily closing prices of Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Binance (BNB), and Ripple (XRP), two fiat-backed stablecoins (USDT and USDC), and a cryptocurrency-collateralised stablecoin (DAI). As a first step, a Granger-causality framework is applied to examine the influence of stablecoin depegging events on crypto returns during financial market stress. The results are strongly asymmetric: there is little evidence that depegs predict returns; whereas cryptocurrency returns robustly Granger-cause USDC depegging events, an effect that intensifies during periods of market stress. Stablecoin depegs appear to be a downstream symptom of cryptocurrency stress rather than a leading indicator of it. The analysis was extended by modelling volatility, using an EGARCH-X model to study whether depegs also affect crypto during periods of market stress and if larger deviations from the dollar peg are associated with higher cryptocurrency volatility, concentrated in the most liquid stablecoins (USDT and USDC), while the evidence for any change in this asso
